[Sociologist](https://www.aeaweb.org/research/du-bois-harvard-marginalists)
and writer, [W.E.B. Du Bois
(1868-1963)](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/dubois/) became nationally
known after 1905’s [Niagara
Movement](https://files.secure.website/wscfus/10207635/32282095/history-of-
the-dubois-circle-from-archives.pdf). He helped form the NAACP in 1909 and the
[Pan-African
Congress](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/24694452.2022.2035667)
during World War I and focused on
[peacemaking](https://africacenter.org/spotlight/pan-africanism-reborn/) and
[decolonization](https://www.un.org/en/global-issues/decolonization). In 1910,
Du Bois served as the editor of [_The Crisis: A Record of the Darker
Races_](https://naacp.org/find-resources/history-explained/history-crisis),
the “[oldest black-oriented journal in the
world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Crisis).” His work that spanned
1910-1934 with the NAACP, [_The Crisis_](https://blackpast.org/african-
american-history/w-e-b-du-bois-close-ranks-editorial-from-the-crisis-
july-1918/), and Pan-Africanism served as his three greatest contributions to
[civil
society](https://scholarlycommons.law.case.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1141&context=swb),
or nongovernmental organizations that advanced the interests of citizens
outside of the government and corporation.

**Du Bois’s Internationalism**

Building on his work from [_The
Crisis_](https://www.marxists.org/history/usa/workers/civil-
rights/crisis/0300-crisis-v01n05-w005.pdf) that addressed human rights abuses
and extrajudicial killings, “[Du Bois as
Diplomat](http://files.hgsitebuilder.com/hostgator881678/file/duboisasdiplomat.pdf)”
wrote timely articles for [_Foreign
Affairs_](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/authors/w-e-b-du-bois) including
“[Worlds of Color](https://cominsitu.wordpress.com/wp-
content/uploads/2019/02/du-bois-worlds-of-color.pdf)” in 1925, where he
explained how European democracy was largely based on exploiting colonial
labor. He cited the Portuguese, Belgian, and French uses of [direct
rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_rule). Du Bois was not only
critical of European racism but pushed back against Senegalese classism as a
form of [indirect violence](https://rpl.hds.harvard.edu/what-we-do/our-
approach/peace-violence).

Further, he wrote about the threats to
[sovereignty](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/liberia/1933-07-01/liberia-
league-and-united-states) in his 1933 essay, “Liberia, the League and the
United States,” and elaborated on global [sovereignty in
Ethiopia](https://cominsitu.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/du-bois-
inter-racial-implications-of-the-ethiopian-crisis-a-negro-view.pdf) in 1935.
By the late 1930s, he shifted his focus to [human and social
development](https://cominsitu.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/du-
bois-black-africa-tomorrow.pdf) in South Africa, Rhodesia, Congo, and Kenya,
and argued for their [economic self-
determination](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/articles/africa/1943-07-01/realities-
africa).

In 1947, as the NAACP representative at the San Francisco [United
Nations](https://read.dukeupress.edu/south-atlantic-quarterly/article-
abstract/123/3/485/389972/Appealing-to-the-World-Du-Bois-and-
the?redirectedFrom=fulltext) Conference, Du Bois helped to write [_An Appeal
to the World!_ _A Statement of Denial of Human Rights to Minorities in the
Case of Citizens of Negro Descent in the United States and an Appeal to the
United Nations for Redress_](https://www.aclu.org/documents/appeal-world). He
historicized systemic oppression and argued that it undermined American
democracy and impacted its ability to take a lead role in protecting colonized
people under an emerging [International Bill of Human
Rights](https://www.ohchr.org/en/what-are-human-rights/international-bill-
human-rights).

Du Bois’s work in 1947 expanded on Marcus Garvey’s 1920 [_Declaration of the
Rights of the Negro Peoples of the World: The Principles of the Universal
Negro Improvement Association_](https://historymatters.gmu.edu/d/5122/). One
article stated:

We demand that our duly accredited representatives be given proper recognition
in all leagues, conferences, conventions or courts of international
arbitration wherever human rights are discussed.

Throughout the 1950s, Du Bois engaged more forcefully in socialist and
communist politics and joined anti-imperialist movements. The FBI started
[surveilling](https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/community.28041093.pdf) him and
his wife [Shirley Graham](https://fbeyes.wustl.edu/items/fbeyes_072.html) in
1942. By 1961, Du Bois moved to Ghana, and he strongly denounced U.S.
capitalism, nationalism, and imperialism. The [Progressive Youth Organizing
Committee](https://www.marxists.org/history/erol/periodicals/mlq-us/pl-
luce.htm) started W.E.B. Du Bois Clubs at the local level from 1959-1963 to
foster political education. After he died in 1963, he left behind a social and
cultural [legacy](https://theberkshireedge.com/great-barringtons-ninth-annual-
du-bois-legacy-festival-to-honor-civil-rights-pioneers-life-and-work/) rooted
in political education continuing into 1964, when the [W.E.B. Du Bois Clubs of
America](https://www.crmvet.org/docs/nor/640000_dubois_flyer2.pdf) were
formally founded by the Communist Party USA, a national youth organization.
His educational [legacy](https://sdonline.org/issue/78/w-e-b-du-
bois%E2%80%99s-legacy-black-radical-intellectual) still provides a
[national](https://abolitionschool.org/) and
[global](https://webduboiscentreaccra.ghana-net.com/)
[presence](https://www.angl.hu-berlin.de/research/conferences/dubois-lectures)
for civil society.

**DCA and Civil Society**

In their initial report on culture and education, the [Du Bois Clubs of
America](https://leninists.org/images/1/1c/War%2C_Racism%2C_the_Movement_As_W_-
_W.E.B._DuBois_Clubs_of_America.pdf) (DCA) adopted a series of measures at the
founding convention in San Francisco on June 21, 1964. The Convention Report
focused on the organization’s internal political education, socialist students
balancing book learning and real-world organizing, cultural commentary, and
resolutions that covered the intersections of power, race, and class.

In the tradition of Du Bois, they emphasized the work of civil society. The
social goal of education was to promote justice and equity, not simply
enjoying elite cultural abstractions, which were void of social struggle. For
example, they referenced [acting](https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-
sound/features/bertolt-brecht-address-danish-worker-actors-art-observation)
and [painting](https://techno-sapien.com/blog/web-dubois-datascience-art) as
two vital skills beyond vocational training and how they could serve as ways
“to defend against brutality and darkness.” In short, students should not be
relegated to an undemocratic technocracy but encouraged to think critically
and challenge domination.

They also targeted segregation, elitism, and the “cult of the [Intelligence
Quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_quotient) and all its
paraphernalia as a sham and an injustice.” They pointed to structural issues
surrounding the role of the guidance counseling office and the privileged
nature of select student groups, fraternities, and sororities rooted in
cultural norms of privilege.

The statement demanded quality education as well as “bread.” They recognized
“the greatest single problem of education is economic, both for institutions
and individuals.” The document called for ending loyalty oath provisions,
military recruitment on campus, and mandatory Cold War curricula. They
considered these hindrances antithetical to academic freedom and democracy
while battling the “ultra-right” and their “quiet takeover of an increasing
number of local educational systems.” DCA members were also pleased to
announce the founding of
[A.I.M.S.](https://a860-collectionguides.nyc.gov/repositories/2/archival_objects/928051),
[The American Institute for Marxist
Studies](https://www.jstor.org/site/reveal-digital/student-
activism/americaninstituteformarxiststudies1967-34007729/?so=item_title_str_asc)
in New York City and stated, “we shall do everything possible to acquaint
students with its purposes, its needs, and the services it offers.”

Additionally, they referred to the impacts of advertisers and [mass
media](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Side_West_Side_\(TV_series\)) and
provided a critique of race culture. At the same time, the club pointed to the
importance of the [Free Southern Theatre](https://snccdigital.org/inside-
sncc/culture-education/free-southern-theater/) at [Tougaloo
College](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_Southern_Theater) in Mississippi,
and the founding of the [Black Arts
Movement](https://www.archives.gov/research/african-americans/black-
power/arts) ([BAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Arts_Movement)). DCA
included a class critique and stated, “race is again only one part of the
larger issue.” “The white worker,” they wrote, “must also discover their image
of dignity in the thickets of violence.” A 1969 edition of the [_Daily
World_](https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/document/swp-us/idb/swp-pc-
min/PC-NEC%20Oct%201968-Mar%201969/20-DuBois-clubs-focus-feb-04-1969.pdf)
reiterated the Du Bois Clubs’ focus on workers.

Their final resolution, number XIV, referenced “Cops” and stated an opposition
to all forms of police brutality including, “local fuzz, the United States
Department of State, and the [Post
Office](https://www.maryferrell.org/php/cryptdb.php?id=HTLINGUAL).” This
included “the stopping of ‘contraband’ literature, and the [interception of
mail](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/DOC_0001420864.pdf) from China,
North Vietnam, and other socialist countries.” The report demonstrated a
general suspicion of civil society work as the _New York Times_ asked in 1966,
“[Are Du Bois Clubs a
Danger?](https://www.nytimes.com/1966/03/13/archives/are-dubois-clubs-a-
danger.html)” At times, the groups faced [internal
fragmentation](https://punctumbooks.com/tag/w-e-b-du-bois-clubs/), or
difficulty in organizing as motions
[failed](https://www.crmvet.org/docs/nor/660000_nsa_clubs.pdf) in specific
clubs subject to both [decline in
membership](https://www.congress.gov/91/crecb/1969/07/09/GPO-
CRECB-1969-pt14-4-3.pdf) and [government
attack](https://www.jstor.org/stable/community.28041089?seq=1). The CIA called
the [Du Bois
Clubs](https://www.archives.gov/files/research/jfk/releases/2022/docid-34530150.pdf)
“[communist controlled](https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/docs/CIA-
RDP75-00149R000500430005-8.pdf)” and
“[subversive](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USREPORTS-389/pdf/USREPORTS-389-309.pdf).”

The [W.E.B. Du Bois Clubs of
America](https://www.nytimes.com/1965/03/15/archives/the-student-left-
spurring-reform-new-activist-intelligentsia-is.html) still have
[reunions](https://www.peoplesworld.org/article/dubois-clubs-reunion-memories-
battles-yet-to-be-fought-and-won/) to celebrate the memory of [local
clubs](https://www.crmvet.org/docs/nor/640000_dubois_flyer.pdf) that spread
across the Lower East Side and Brooklyn, as well as Albuquerque, Madison,
[Berkeley](https://www.crmvet.org/docs/nor/640000_dubois_flyer2.pdf), [Los
Angeles](https://www.crmvet.org/docs/nor/650900_dubois_newsletter.pdf), [San
Jose](https://www.archives.gov/files/research/jfk/releases/2022/docid-34517446.pdf),
[East Lansing](https://www.facebook.com/MSUDuboisSociety/), Chicago,
Minneapolis, and Philadelphia. These groups galvanized around local, state,
federal and
[international](https://assets.cambridge.org/97811084/91648/frontmatter/9781108491648_frontmatter.pdf)
issues that included a fair economy, health care,
[independence](https://www.nytimes.com/1964/10/24/archives/taiwan-accuses-
professor-of-independence-activity.html), and issues of war and peace in
[Vietnam](https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/document/swp-us/idb/swp-pc-
min/PC%20Apr%201964-Sep%201966/25-end-the-war-in-Vietnam-nov-25-28-1965.pdf).

[Bettina Aptheker and Angela
Davis](https://www.jstor.org/stable/10.7591/j.ctt5hh0g9) were prominent
leaders of the club as were [Terrence
Hallinan](https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/document/swp-us/idb/swp-pc-
min/PC%20Apr%201964-Sep%201966/27-report-dubois-clubs-org.pdf), serving as
West Coast coordinator, and [Jarvis
Tyner](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/08854300.2018.1558898),
another well-known coordinator located in
[Philadelphia](https://www.marxists.org/history/etol/document/swp-us/idb/swp-
pc-min/PC%20Apr%201964-Sep%201966/24-summary-of-WEB-Dubois-club-
dec-2-4-1965.pdf). This CSO work was not the safest and usually carried a
risk. For example, its national headquarters in [San
Francisco](https://www.wisconsinhistory.org/Records/Image/IM54996) was bombed
in 1966.

**Du Bois Movement School**

Although the W.E.B. Du Bois Clubs of America were largely challenges to Cold
War liberalism through the mobilization of Marxist youth, today’s [W.E.B. Du
Bois Movement School for Abolition &
Reconstruction](https://abolitionschool.org/) is a political education program
based in West Philadelphia, “designed for aspiring revolutionaries and
movement leaders from communities most impacted by poverty, policing, and mass
incarceration.” The program “emerged in the wake of the 2020 uprisings
following [George Floyd’s murder in
Minneapolis](https://www.un.org/en/yearbook/eliminating-racism-time-change),
when many people were eager to engage with questions of abolition but lacked
the framework and historical grounding to do so.”

As a result of 2020, [140 new oversight laws](https://www.vera.org/news/five-
years-after-george-floyds-murder-whats-changed) were passed. In linking the
earlier [Du Bois clubs](https://firstamendment.mtsu.edu/article/w-e-b-dubois-
clubs-of-america-v-clark/) and forms of civil society and political education,
the Du Bois Abolition School features “organic intellectuals,” who seek to
“not only understand the world, but to actively transform it.”

The school’s coordinator is writer and organizer, Geo Maher, the author of [_A
World Without Police and Anticolonial Eruptions: How Strong Communities Make
Cops Obsolete_](https://geomaher.com/a-world-without-police/) (Verso, 2021).
[Christopher R. Rogers](https://www.wewinfromwithin.com/), a professor from
Chester, PA and a national steering committee member for Black Lives Matter
also serves on the leadership team. They work alongside Philadelphia natives
and facilitators [Nneka Azuka](https://abolitionjournal.com/movement-moments-
pao-rally-speech-%7C-nneka-azuka) and Anthony Smith of the Black Philly
Radical Collective. Another community organizer and advocate is [Saudia
Durrant](https://facingrace.raceforward.org/speaker/saudia-durrant) with the
[Gender Justice Fund](https://www.genderjusticephilly.com/history). All these
individuals that work on [abolition in
Philadelphia](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=55pgx42NPIU) emphasize the
importance of local history and the meaning of figures like [Mumia Abu-
Jamal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mumia_Abu-Jamal) and [Russell Maroon
Shoatz](https://pmpress.org/index.php?l=product_detail&p=541) extending
globally.

**Epilogue**

Du Bois’s early civil society work was not without
[criticism](https://revolutionsnewsstand.com/2023/05/04/the-descent-of-du-
bois-1918-by-hubert-h-harrison-when-africa-awakes-porro-press-new-york-
city-1920/). The tradeoff for acquiring early forms of [soft
power](https://education.cfr.org/learn/reading/what-soft-power) for racial
uplift via the “talented tenth” included gradualism in ending World War I,
hesitancy on addressing anti-lynching laws, and ultimately support for Woodrow
Wilson, arguably the most openly racist modern president. The person that
highlighted these class-based critiques most effectively was [Hubert
Harrison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hubert_Harrison).

Over time, Du Bois moved closer to Harrison politically. The fact that present
day abolitionists also devote their time to [international
affairs](https://www.npr.org/2021/06/07/1003872848/the-complicated-history-
behind-blms-solidarity-with-the-pro-palestinian-movement) is emblematic of the
“[Du Bois Doctrine](https://www.foreignaffairs.com/united-states/web-du-bois-
doctrine-race-america-century)” and an ability to link his formative theories
with his later radical [global
politics](https://press.princeton.edu/books/hardcover/9780691179155/worldmaking-
after-
empire?srsltid=AfmBOorQXO6UAuHaEKGanB8SiWSkLAR-f3wWVGoyUc3NAlfwFA7unKVb). Du
Bois’s thoughts on [democracy and
empire](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/w-e-b-du-bois-international-
thought/democracy-and-empire/76CCFD6BA9048169C184489513B03BA8) connect
[his](https://cominsitu.wordpress.com/wp-content/uploads/2019/02/w-e-b-du-
bois-web-du-bois-speaks-speeches-and-addresses-18901919-1.pdf) [radical
legacy](https://digitalcommons.law.uw.edu/wlr/vol99/iss2/5/) in protesting
state violence with international issues, [civil society
work](https://abolitionschool.org/donate/), and the “[politics of
care](https://dissentmagazine.org/article/abolition-as-method/).”

U.S. cities have reorganized their methods in public safety since the 2020
George Floyd uprisings and reforms in places like [Minneapolis and
Louisville](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/justice-department-moves-to-
cancel-minneapolis-and-louisville-police-reform-settlements) currently face
resistance. Cities such as [New York](https://www.nyc.gov/mayors-
office/news/2025/11/mayor-adams-releases-november-2025-financial-plan-update-
with-ne) and [Los
Angeles](https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-01-21/council-approves-
lapd-hiring-boost-despite-budget-concerns) have reestablished their police
funding after considering cuts, but some [alternative
crisis](https://www.themarshallproject.org/2024/07/25/police-mental-health-
alternative-911) response programs conducted by civil society in the spirit of
Du Bois [remain](https://mindsitenews.org/2025/07/25/chicago-crisis-response-
program-at-tipping-point/). Reform [has not
disappeared](https://www.cbsnews.com/newyork/news/nyc-mayor-zohran-mamdani-
nypd-enrollment-eric-adams/), but its momentum has been disrupted in an era of
[vigilantism](https://www.democracynow.org/2026/2/19/ice_jailed_people_illegally)and
the dismantling of [federal oversight](https://www.naacpldf.org/case-
issue/president-trumps-executive-order-on-policing-explained/). Activism is
messy. Struggle is never to be abandoned, only reconfigured moving forward in
the tradition of Du Bois.
